newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singaporeans vote for prosperity, shun principles.
newsitem.headline: Singaporeans vote for prosperity, shun principles.

text.p: Singaporeans handed the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) a massive general election win because they prefer material prosperity to abstract principles of democracy, analysts and newspapers said on Friday.

"More than anything else, yesterday's poll result demonstrates that the Singaporean is, first and foremost, a practical creature who not only knows on which side his bread is buttered but also wants his bread to be buttered generously," the Business Times said in a front page editorial on Friday.

The opposition agreed with regret. "We have fought on basic ideals...It confirms that materialism is part of Singapore and I feel very sad. Because, without a soul, a country cannot sustain itself," said Wong Wee Nam, a member of an opposition slate that crashed to defeat in a multi-seat constituency.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong trumpeted the near PAP sweep as a rejection by voters of the liberal democracy championed by the West. The PAP won 81 of the 83 seats at stake in parliament.
"They have rejected rejected Western-style liberal democracy and freedoms, putting individual rights over that of society," Goh told a post-victory news conference.

He said the two leading opposition figures who lost in the polls, Chee Soon Juan of the Singapore Democratic Party and Joshua Jeyaretnam of the Workers' Party, had tried and failed to "sell these Western agendas, promoted by the Western media and pressure groups like (human rights group) AsiaWatch."
"This is consistent with the (government) philosophy they've been trying to develop over the past few years," said Bruce Gale, analyst at Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
The result indicated that Singaporeans had opted for the stability represented by the PAP, he added.
While annoyed at the often heavy-handed attitude of the PAP, most Singaporeans voted them in anyway.
"For all my grouses, I cannot cut my nose to spite my face. I will vote for the PAP," a 60-year-old resident of a public housing estate said before casting his vote.
A 27-year-old owner of two apartments said bluntly there was no reason to change a good thing. "I've done very well under the PAP," he said.
"A lot of them expressed dissatisfaction with the PAP, but they voted for them anyway. It seems to boil down to political stability," Gale said.
The PAP's huge win can also be attributed to the strength of its own candidates, he added.
"I think they were voting on personalities," Gale said. "The guy who made the most talk about rights is Jeyaretnam and he lost, along with his friends."
It also did not hurt that the PAP used hardball tactics in the brief nine-day election campaign to remind voters forcefully of the consequences of voting for the opposition.
Goh told voters bluntly they risked losing out on the multi-billion dollar upgrading of public housing where nearly 80 percent of all Singaporeans live if they voted in the opposition.
It also brought all its force to bear to keep one man -- Tang Liang Hong of the Workers' Party -- out of parliament.
The PAP accused Tang of being a Chinese chauvinist and Goh quoted the opposition politician as saying ethnic Chinese were "carrying the sedan chair" instead of sitting in it.

"The deep fault lines in our society over race, language, culture and religion will not go away. We must manage these emotional issues carefully," Goh said. "We are not a Chinese country and must never allow Chinese chauvinists to turn us into one."
Tang was on a five-member Workers' Party team which lost a close race with the PAP in a winner-take-all battle. The PAP won with a little less than 55 percent of the vote.

Tang said the allegations were "nonsense" while party mate Low Thia Khiang called the use of the racial card by the PAP a "tactic" which showed that opposition candidates in Singapore face a great risk and pay a high price when they seek election.
